subtype: Approach: working out what actually happened [Thinking]
passage: That night Kabir lay on his bed, replaying Tuesday. His friend Farhan's tiffin had slipped off the desk and the rice went everywhere. Kabir had laughed, loudly. Farhan had gone very still, then shouted, "You always mock me!" and marched off to the playground. Kabir's first thought was: he's overreacting, it was funny. But he ran the scene back slowly. Farhan on his knees, picking rice out of the dust. The whole class watching. And Kabir's laugh, the loudest one. He sat up. If that were his own tiffin, he would be furious too. Tomorrow he would not start with "you were unfair." He would start with what he had done.

qa.q: What did Kabir do when Farhan's tiffin fell?
How did Kabir's thinking change as he replayed the scene?
qa.a: Kabir first thought Farhan was overreacting, then felt guilty and understood how mocked Farhan must have felt.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Kabir try tomorrow, and why?
qa.a: Kabir could say sorry for the laugh and explain there was no mean intention, because the hurt comes first. Offering to help or share lunch could also show care.

qa.q: How does the moment look to Farhan?
qa.a: Farhan was kneeling in front of the class, picking up rice, and heard the loudest laugh from Kabir, so it felt like being mocked by a friend.

grounding: A boy replays the quarrel, realises his laugh at the dropped tiffin felt like mockery and sees the friend's side.

passage:
"Why isn't Manav talking to you?" Jasleen asked, dropping onto the sofa.
"No idea. He just walked off at lunch."
"What happened at lunch?"
Siddharth thought. "Nothing. We were in the line... his tiffin fell. The lid flew off, rajma everywhere."
"And?"
"And I laughed. But not at him! The lid spun like a top. It was funny."
"Did he know that?"
Siddharth went quiet. "Everyone was looking. His shirt had rajma on it." He rubbed his face. "He thought I was laughing at him."
"So?"
"So I don't want to ask 'Why are you angry?' any more. I want to say sorry. And share my lunch with him tomorrow."

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he went quiet and rubbed his face?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and sorry, realising Manav thought he was being laughed at.

qa.q: What else could Siddharth say to Manav?
qa.a: That he laughed at the spinning lid, not at Manav, but leading with the sorry; seeing Manav's side changed what he wants to say.

qa.q: How did the moment in the line feel for Manav?
qa.a: With everyone looking and rajma on his shirt, Manav probably felt embarrassed and hurt, and Siddharth's laugh felt like mockery.

grounding: Shows a boy thinking back over a quarrel, realising he laughed when his friend's tiffin fell, and seeing why the friend felt mocked.

subtype: Approach: working out what actually happened [Thinking]
passage: Last week Anand stopped sitting with me on the bus, and at first I was angry at him. What did I do? That night I lay awake and replayed the whole day like a video. Morning: fine. Maths: fine. Lunch: Anand tripped on the step and his tiffin burst open, idlis rolling across the floor. And I laughed. I remember now, I laughed loudly, because one idli rolled right into the Principal's office. But Anand didn't see that idli. He only saw his lunch on the floor and me laughing. No wonder. The next morning I didn't ask why he was sulking. I said, 'I wasn't laughing at you, but I shouldn't have laughed. Sorry.' He looked at me a long time, then said, 'Okay, Siddharth bhai. Sit.'

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel at first when Anand stopped sitting with him?
qa.a: Siddharth felt angry and confused, not understanding what he had done.

qa.q: What made Siddharth's apology better than asking why Anand was sulking?
qa.a: It showed he understood Anand's side, that his laugh looked like mockery, instead of blaming Anand for sulking.

qa.q: How did the lunch moment look from Anand's side?
qa.a: Anand only saw his lunch on the floor and Siddharth laughing loudly, so Anand likely felt humiliated and mocked.

grounding: Illustrates a boy replaying a quarrel, realising his laugh when his friend dropped his tiffin looked like mockery, and changing what he says.
